US stocks remained on a cautious footing Monday following the S&P 500’s worst week since April 2025, with support from cheaper oil prices offset by continued pressure on chipmakers.
Futures for the US benchmark rose 0.1%, while those for the Nasdaq 100 fell 0.4%. Nvidia Corp. dropped about 6% on Tradegate after Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang’s admission of an affair with a woman identified as a suspected Chinese spy. The chip giant’s board has launched an investigation.

A group of Thames Water creditors agreed to back plans to push out debt repayments, buying more time to agree on a broader rescue for the troubled utility.
The UK’s largest water and sewerage company said Monday that creditors holding more than £12 billion ($16.1 billion) of secured debt supported a proposal to move repayments due next year into 2028, but it still needs approval through a court-supervised restructuring process.

Intercontinental Exchange Inc. is launching new wind derivatives, joining a growing wave of exchanges trying to turn weather volatility into a more easily traded financial risk as renewable power reshapes electricity markets.
The contracts, announced Monday in a market notice, will cover Germany, the UK, France, Denmark, Italy, the Netherlands and Spain. ICE says the futures will cover 70% of Europe’s wind generation capacity and include onshore and offshore production. The contracts are set to go live on Dec. 14, pending regulatory approval.

Nigeria’s top lender by assets is considering exiting at least one of its foreign markets as the business with operations in about 24 countries looks to comply with central-bank rules limiting external investments.
Access Holdings Plc has identified one “troublesome” business that it may dispose of to meet the regulations, Chairman Aigboje Aig-Imoukhuede said.

By Janice Huang and Aileen ChuangNovember 9, 2026 at 6:37 AM UTCUpdated on November 9, 2026 at 7:23 AM UTCBookmark
Save
Takeaways by Bloomberg AI
Alphabet Inc. has had talks recently about potentially offering its first Hong Kong and Singapore dollar bonds, people familiar with the matter said, a deal that would test investor appetite in Asia after an AI selloff in global markets.
The Google parent had spoken with banks and investors about a debt sale as early as this month, the people said, asking not to be identified discussing private matters. The company is looking to raise the equivalent of $1 billion to $1.5 billion in Hong Kong dollars and around $1.5 billion in Singapore dollars, the people said. Proceeds would be used for general corporate purposes, they added.
